html:
On 4 August 2020 about 2,750 tonnes of ammonium nitrate stored at the port of Beirut exploded after a fire. It killed more than 200 people, injured about 7,000 and wrecked much of the city around the port.

The chemical, used for fertiliser and explosives, had been taken off a ship, the Rhosus, in 2014 and kept in a warehouse for six years. Port, customs and court officials had written many letters about it; nothing was done. The blast was one of the largest non-nuclear explosions ever recorded. It flattened the port's grain silos, shattered windows kilometres away and left some 300,000 people homeless.

It came as Lebanon was already in deep economic collapse, with banks freezing savings, the currency crashing and the COVID-19 pandemic spreading. The government resigned within days. Lebanon's sectarian system of shared power, set up by the National Pact of 1943, was blamed for protecting the powerful. The judge leading the inquiry was blocked again and again by politicians, and no one has yet been held to account. Compare the Halifax explosion of 1917.
